rv.q: Dragging himself to the piano, he throws himself at the keys with a violence and a delicacy that makes his inspired take on Gershwin’s Rhapsody In Blue an almost unbearably eloquent expression of syncopated heartbreak, the sound of a soul under siege.
Doug Wright’s play is a fast-paced, highly polished, zinger-packed vehicle for his astonishing performance...

Director Lisa Peterson gives the production a slick, effective staging, conveying both the exhilarating momentum and crushing time pressure of a live broadcast, with assistants charging between dressing rooms and studio execs arguing as they try to wrangle the talent.

What sets this dazzling, considered Tony award-winning Broadway transfer apart is the fantastically energised performance from Sean Hayes, best known to TV viewers as the flamboyant best friend Jack in the sitcom Will & Grace.
It’s hauntingly powerful and the apex of this funny and devastating play.
Doug Wright’s script is zippy, fast-paced and very funny (this is gag-a-minute comedy betting on the law of numbers).
His sensational performance lifts the evening into something truly blue, truly rhapsodic.

Levant, a great wit and even greater pianist, had charisma that could swallow a room, so it’s to the writer Doug Wright’s credit that his play captures that, as well as the rise of the late-night talk show, explaining why Levant sacrificed his fragile mental health to appear on one.

Lisa Peterson’s slick, whizzy production, co-starring Rosalie Craig as Levant’s wife June, is a thrilling theatrical experience but, perhaps perversely for a play arguing for television to be more serious, does not bear looking at too closely.

This play might be satirising the media world that exploited and destroyed Levant, but it nonetheless falls into the same trap – of delivering a glimmering, beguiling surface without looking too hard at what’s going on underneath.
Yet we leave this 100-minute play no wiser as to the real man behind this troubled facade.

Sean Hayes, Tony Award in stowage, crosses The Atlantic to reprise his role as Levant and it’s hard to overstate just how good he is, a one-man rebuttal for the disappointments many have felt paying top dollar for big Hollywood names in the West End.
This is a rare and glorious kind of show.
Doug Wright's extremely entertaining and tightly wound play Good Night, Oscar
A delightful, memorable and charming night out.
Hayes's brilliance elevates it into a must-see.
Ultimately, Good Night, Oscar is a solid piece of non-nonsense bioplay made brilliant by an unmissable Hayes.
Even so, his is an extraordinary performance, the unmasking of a genuinely sad clown with a great capacity for melancholy and, one hopes, future meaty roles.
Hayes is a classically trained pianist; when it comes, it is passionate and exciting.
